note: Vol. I No. 26. A legible marine list under the heading PORT OF CHICAGO, the Fort Dearborn beef contract that names the fort's store house as the delivery point, a school district calling its voters to the school house, and a hatter who has come to town to put up a factory at the corner of Lake street.

claims.notes: THE PORT OF CHICAGO UNDER ITS OWN HEADING, and legible enough to count. Six or seven movements in the last ten days of May 1834, and the trade is SHORT-HAUL LAKE TRAFFIC: St. Joseph across the lake, Detroit, Green Bay. The rigs are the small ones — schooners, a SLOOP (the Dart, Barnard, in twice), one brig — which is what a harbour with a bar across its mouth could take in 1834, and it bounds the size of hull this reconstruction may moor at the river wharves. The brig John Kinzie shares a name with the forwarding merchant advertising three columns away, and the two are NOT identified with one another here beyond the coincidence of the name. Three passengers are entered on one arrival, so the same hulls carried people. Several entries are cut and the ones that are stay bracketed rather than repaired.

claims.notes: THERE IS A SCHOOL HOUSE IN CHICAGO IN MAY 1834 AND IT IS THE DISTRICT'S MEETING ROOM. The notice does not describe the building; it does something better for dating purposes — it assumes it. A school district with trustees, voters and a house to meet in is a going institution, and the meeting is called there rather than at a tavern, which is where the militia election of the same month had to be held (chicago_democrat_1834_05_14 c006). So by May 1834 the town has at least one purpose-built or purpose-taken public room. The district number and the school house's location are both cut and are NOT supplied. P. Pruyne signs, the third notice over his name this month.

Teeth 'properly cleansed and filled with gold' in Chicago in May 1834 is a small fact about how much town there was to support it. claims.notes: A NEW STORE ON DEARBORN STREET, ONE DOOR FROM NEWBERRY & DOLE'S. This is the fourth advertiser in one month to fix himself off Newberry & Dole (see chicago_democrat_1834_05_07 c003 and c005, and c008 here in the same issue), and it is the one that puts a STREET NAME to the forwarding house's neighbourhood: Dearborn street. Newberry & Dole place themselves 'opposite to Fort Dearborn'; W. H. Brown places himself one door from them, on Dearborn street. The two statements are compatible and together they tie a stretch of Dearborn street to the fort's frontage, which is a thing the reconstruction's street layer can use. The word after 'one' is cut and 'door' is supplied only in the normalized reading, where the count of doors is the conventional form of the phrase in every other Chicago advertisement in this month; the quote leaves it out.

claims.notes: A MANUFACTORY IS ABOUT TO BE BUILT, AND THE PAPER SAYS SO IN ADVANCE. A hatter has moved to Chicago and INTENDS TO PUT UP A FACTORY — a stated future building, dated May 1834, on the record before it exists. For a reconstruction that is a rare thing: a construction intention with a date and a trade attached, which either was or was not carried out by the scene date and can be looked for. Meanwhile he sells from the CORNER OF LAKE STREET, opposite Dr. Temple's — the second advertiser this month to use Temple's as the anchor (chicago_democrat_1834_05_14 c002), confirming it as a Lake street landmark. The cross street at the corner is cut and is NOT supplied, so the placement is recorded as a corner on Lake with Temple's as its anchor and one arm unknown. Hats in black, brown and drab, of his own making: three colours is what a Chicago head wore.

claims.notes: THE FORT'S STORE HOUSE IS THE DELIVERY DOOR, AND THE GARRISON IS SIZED BY ITS BEEF. Two hard facts for the Fort Dearborn model, both stated and neither inferred. FIRST: a building called THE STORE HOUSE OF FORT DEARBORN exists on 26 May 1834 and is the point at which quartered beef is received — so it is a provision store with cart access, which is a placement constraint (it must front something a beef wagon can reach) and a use, not just a footprint on a plan. The reconstruction's fort currently builds its ranges without distinguishing what they were for; this names one. SECOND: 'probably 400 pounds per week' of fresh beef, delivered one to three times a week for a year from 20 June 1834. At the army ration of the period that is a garrison in the low hundreds at most — the arithmetic is NOT done here and no headcount is claimed, because the ration rate is not in this document; what the line does establish is that the post was provisioned continuously by CIVILIAN CONTRACT from the surrounding country, on a bid advertised in the town's own newspaper, which is a relationship between fort and town worth drawing. The contracting officer's name survives only as an initial and is NOT supplied; he is a lieutenant of the 5th Infantry acting as Assistant Commissary of Subsistence.

Filer & Co on 21 May (chicago_democrat_1834_05_21 c003), Clark, Filer & Co on 28 May, and the premises are 'the cabinet shop' — definite article, no address, because by now the reader knows which one. That is a shop established enough in four weeks to be THE cabinet shop of the town. The two firm names are recorded as they are printed and are NOT merged into one entry here: Filer is common to both and the identity is likely, but identity is identity.json's business and not a reading pass's.

claims.notes: A NAMED STOREFRONT AT THE EAST END OF SOUTH WATER STREET, WITH ITS PREVIOUS OCCUPANT NAMED. This is the 'building lately occupied by…' chain the epic asks for, in its cleanest May 1834 form: the premises pass from Peter Cohen to Doty & Co, are FITTED UP as a dry goods store, and are located by the end of the street rather than by a cross-street. 'The east end of South Water-street' is a placement the reconstruction's South Water frontage can act on — it is the river-mouth end, the end nearest the fort and the wharves, and it is where the month's salt came off (chicago_democrat_1834_05_14 c003). Two proprietors in a row in one building is also the clearest evidence in the month that South Water shopfronts turned over fast, which is what a survival liberty reaching to 1835 has to reckon with. The same advertisement stands in the 21 May issue.

claims.notes: A CORNER PLACEMENT ON SOUTH WATER, AND THE ONLY ONE IN THE MONTH THAT NAMES BOTH STREETS. Franklin and South Water: an attorney's office standing at that intersection, advertised continuously since December 1833 and still running in May 1834. Franklin is at the WEST end of the platted South Water frontage, so with Doty & Co at the east end (claim c008) the month's two firmest South Water addresses bracket the street. An attorney's office is a small tenancy — one room — and it is the kind of use the reconstruction currently has no record for on a corner lot.

claims.notes: ONE IMPRESSION OF THE STANDING LAKE STREET LAND-AGENCY CARD. The Democrat sets this advertisement, word for word the same, in every issue from 1834-05-14 to 1834-10-01 — twenty consecutive weeks, eighteen of which set the line ‘purchased and Sold, or by commi[s]sion’ recognisably (T-1051). The card is identified by its copy and not by its display line: the same trade (‘House and Land Agent’), the same offer of building lots in the town and the School Section, the same houses to let, and the same office on Lake street opposite Dr. Temple's. The display line survives as 'hr Gh' (line 2861) in another Tesseract-fallback column (the flag is line 2860) and nothing can be read off it. THE PROPRIETOR'S NAME IS NOT READ HERE and none is supplied into the quote: the record's ‘W. G. Blanchard’ stands on T-0408's reading of the two impressions whose columns are NOT Tesseract fallbacks (1834-07-16 line 5527, 1834-09-17 line 3292) and on identity.json's declared firm merge, not on this impression. THE STREET IS NOT SET HERE: the address line reads 'at. opposite Dr. Temple's.' and the word 'Lake' did not survive the left margin, so the anchor is read and the street is left null rather than carried in from the weeks either side. 'R' at line 2864 and the trailing 'ee'/'ae' are margin droppings of the fallback column, quoted where they stand rather than cleaned away.
